objectives: Say what waste is.
Say how much waste cities make.
Name the biggest kinds of city waste.
Use may for the future.
content.pedagogy: The opening chapter defines waste and gives the big numbers. A number card (2023 → 2050) helps learners hold the facts. The last paragraph turns the problem into a chance: waste can still be useful.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “Billion” is 1,000 million.
“May” shows a possibility, not a fact.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: may + base verb · more than
Look (Activity 1): By 2050, this number may be nearly 4 billion tons.
Practise (Activity 2): fill than, may and fast.
Likely errors: *may is · *more that.
Use (Activity 3): my waste today.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Numbers: two billion tons; four billion tons; twenty twenty-three.
Stress: BIL-lion, RE-cy-cling, col-LECT.
beforeReading: Ask: “What did you throw away today?”
duringReading: First reading: What is waste?
Second reading: complete the number card.
Find what is still useful.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–16 Number card; 16–20 Quick Challenge; 20–32 Language Focus 1–2; 32–38 Use: my waste today; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What is waste?
Why is plastic waste a problem?
Why is waste not only a problem?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “2 Billion Tons” and “Still Useful” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: waste, throw away, tons, trash, collect, recycling.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the number card with the years written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write four sentences about waste in your town with may.

expectedResponses: Waste is anything that we don’t want or need anymore. In 2023, people in cities made more than 2 billion tons of waste. By 2050, this number may be nearly 4 billion tons.
content.transferTask: Write about the waste you made today.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners see waste as both a problem and a resource?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “may” about waste in 2050.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners say three sentences about waste in the world today. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A reads paragraphs 1 and 2, B reads paragraphs 3 and 4. Each tells the partner two facts without looking. The partner writes them down, then both check in the text.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Groups of three. Reader reads paragraph 3. Asker asks “What is most of the waste in cities?” Checker checks the answer.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A younger child asks, “What is waste?” The learner answers in two short sentences with an example.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “Many things in our trash are still useful.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, what waste is and why it is a big problem. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “The chapter says waste is a problem. Then it says ‘But waste is not only a problem.’ What is the other side?” (Many things can be used again.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners explain “waste” in their own words and give the numbers for 2023 and 2050.

thinkAloud.sentence: Waste is anything that we don’t want or need anymore.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: “Waste is” tells me this is a definition. I can use it to explain the word to someone else. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “In 2023, people in cities made more than 2 billion tons of waste.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: How much waste may there be by 2050?

onlineTask.post: Write two sentences: What do you throw away most at home?

objectives: Say where paper, wood and glass come from.
Explain how each one is recycled.
Explain why glass recycling helps nature.
Use is made from and steps in the present simple.
content.pedagogy: The chapter has one paragraph for each material. A three-column chart (Paper · Wood · Glass) with “comes from” and “becomes” helps learners compare.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Paper and wood both come from trees; glass comes from sand.
Glass is sorted by color, not by size.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: is made from · comes from · present simple for steps (sort → melt → make)
Look (Activity 1): Glass is made from sand …
Practise (Activity 2): sort the glass steps.
Likely errors: *is made of from · *workers sorts.
Use (Activity 3): our bins.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Stress: SEP-a-rate (adjective), FUR-ni-ture, MA-te-ri-als.
Sound: jar /dʒɑːr/.
duringReading: First reading: Where do paper, wood and glass come from?
Second reading: complete the three-column chart.
Put the glass steps in order.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–16 Three-column chart; 16–20 Quick Challenge; 20–32 Language Focus 1–2; 32–38 Use: our bins; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why must paper waste stay dry?
What can old wood become?
How does glass recycling help nature?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “A Separate Bin” and “Sorted by Color” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: separate, bin, recycling center, board, jar, sort, melt.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with the headings written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write the steps for recycling paper.

formativeAssessment: Says where each material comes from.
expectedResponses: Glass is made from sand and some other natural materials. Workers sort the glass by color. Then they melt it and make new bottles and jars.
content.transferTask: Write about recycling at your school.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners compare the three materials?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “is made from”.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners explain how paper, wood and glass are recycled. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A reads about paper and wood, B reads about glass. Each tells the partner how the material is recycled.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the paragraph about glass. Asker asks “How do workers sort the glass?” Checker checks the answer.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A neighbor puts glass bottles in the normal trash. The learner explains politely where they should go.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “When we recycle paper, we need fewer new trees.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, how paper, wood and glass are recycled. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “Why must paper waste stay dry?” (Wet paper cannot be recycled well.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners give the steps for glass in the right order: collect, sort, melt, make.

thinkAloud.sentence: Then they melt it and make new bottles and jars.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: “Then” shows the next step after sorting. I can write the steps for glass as a list. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “Paper comes from trees in forests.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: What does old wood become in recycling centers?

onlineTask.post: Write two sentences: Where do you put paper and glass at school?

objectives: Say why plastic is hard to recycle.
Say how plastic production grew.
Say what happened to plastic waste in 2019.
Use the past simple and percent.
content.pedagogy: The chapter gives clear numbers. A pie chart (9 · 19 · 50 · 22) helps learners see where plastic waste went. The numbers add up to 100.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Only 9 percent was recycled; half went into landfills.
“Twice as much” means two times more.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: past simple (recycled, burned, went, stayed) · percent · twice as much
Look (Activity 1): People recycled only 9 percent of it.
Practise (Activity 2): match the numbers.
Likely errors: *burn 19 percent (past) · *goed.
Use (Activity 3): my plastic yesterday.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Numbers: nine percent; nineteen percent; three hundred fifty million tons.
Endings: recycled /d/, burned /d/, stayed /d/.
beforeReading: Ask: “Where does plastic go after we throw it away?”
duringReading: First reading: Why is plastic hard to recycle?
Second reading: complete the pie chart.
Find what a landfill is.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–16 Pie chart; 16–20 Quick Challenge; 20–32 Language Focus 1–2; 32–38 Use: my plastic yesterday; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why is plastic everywhere?
What happened to half of the plastic waste?
Why is plastic waste a very big problem?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Twice as Much Plastic” and “Landfills” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: plastic, twice as much, percent, burn, landfill, nature.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the pie chart with the numbers written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short news report about plastic waste in 2019.

formativeAssessment: Explains why plastic is hard to recycle.
expectedResponses: There are many kinds of plastic, so we can’t recycle all of them in the same way. In 2019, people recycled only 9 percent of plastic waste. Half of it went into landfills.
content.transferTask: Write about the plastic you used yesterday.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners read the numbers correctly?

exitTicket: Write one sentence about plastic in 2019 with the past simple.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains why plastic is hard to recycle.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners explain what happens to plastic waste. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: One learner reads paragraph 3 and tells a partner the four numbers. The partner draws a simple chart.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the sentence about landfills. Asker asks “What is a landfill?” Checker finds the meaning.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A friend asks, “Why is plastic a big problem?” The learner answers with two numbers from the chapter.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “That is why plastic waste is a very big problem today.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, what happens to plastic waste in the world. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “Only 9 percent was recycled. Why is this number important?” (Most plastic is not recycled.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners give the four percentages correctly and explain “landfill”.

thinkAloud.strategy: Find the meaning in the next sentence
thinkAloud.sentence: Landfills are big places where people put trash under the ground.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: The sentence before uses “landfills”. This sentence explains it. So I do not need a dictionary. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “Plastic is everywhere.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: How much plastic waste did the world have in 2019?

onlineTask.post: Write two sentences: How can you use less plastic?
onlineTask.reply: Give your classmate one more idea.

objectives: Say what cartons are made of.
Explain how cartons and metal are recycled.
Explain why recycling metal is a good idea.
Use must and much less … than.
content.pedagogy: The chapter has two materials: cartons and metal. A two-column chart (Carton / Metal) with “made of” and “what happens” helps learners compare. The question “Is recycling metal a good idea?” models a simple argument.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Cartons are not only paper; they also have plastic and sometimes metal.
“Much less” makes the difference bigger.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: must + base verb · much less … than · be made of
Look (Activity 1): People must collect it separately.
Practise (Activity 2): fill paper, metal and from.
Likely errors: *must to collect · *less energy that.
Use (Activity 3): our kitchen.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: CAR-ton, PACK-ag-ing, SEP-a-rate-ly, EN-er-gy.
beforeReading: Ask: “What is a milk carton made of?”
duringReading: First reading: What are cartons made of?
Second reading: complete the two-column chart.
Find why recycling metal is good.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–16 Two-column chart; 16–20 Quick Challenge; 20–32 Language Focus 1–2; 32–38 Use: our kitchen; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why does carton packaging make a lot of waste?
Where does metal come from?
Why is recycling metal a good idea?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Paper and Plastic Together” and “Much Less Energy” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: carton, packaging, separately, product, can, energy.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with the headings written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write four sentences about recycling cartons and cans.

formativeAssessment: Says what cartons are made of.
Explains why recycling metal is good.
expectedResponses: Juice and milk cartons are made of paper and plastic together. People must collect them separately. Recycling metal uses much less energy than taking new metal from the earth.
content.transferTask: Write about cartons and cans in your kitchen.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners compare cartons and metal?

rubricLevels.secure: Says what cartons are made of.
Explains why recycling metal is good.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners explain how cartons and metal are recycled. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A reads paragraph 1 and B reads paragraphs 2 and 3. Each tells the partner the main idea.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the last two sentences. Asker asks “Why is recycling metal a good idea?” Checker finds the answer.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A family member asks, “Is a milk carton paper or plastic?” The learner answers using the chapter.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “It uses much less energy than taking new metal from the earth.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, how cartons and metal cans are recycled. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “Why must people collect cartons separately?” (They are made of different materials.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners name the materials in a carton and give one example of metal waste.

thinkAloud.sentence: It uses much less energy than taking new metal from the earth.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: “Less … than” compares two ways. Recycling metal uses less energy. So recycling is the better way. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “Juice and milk cartons are made of paper and plastic together.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: What do workers do with old metal?

onlineTask.post: Write two sentences: Which cans do you use at home?

objectives: Say what cooking oil is made from.
Explain what happens to old oil.
Say where food waste happens.
Use is called and is lost / is wasted.
content.pedagogy: The chapter has two parts: cooking oil and food. The numbers (13 · 17 · 61) surprise learners: most food waste happens at home. This makes the topic personal.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Biodiesel is made from old plant oil, not from oil under the ground.
61 percent is the part of food waste that happens at home, not 61 percent of all food.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: is called · is lost / is wasted · must
Look (Activity 1): This fuel is called biodiesel.
Practise (Activity 2): fill lost, wasted and home.
Likely errors: *is call · *is waste.
Use (Activity 3): less food waste.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Stress: BI-o-die-sel, SUN-flow-ers, VEG-e-ta-bles, RES-tau-rants.
Numbers: sixty-one percent.
beforeReading: Ask: “What do you do with old cooking oil at home?”
duringReading: First reading: What happens to old oil?
Second reading: complete the food waste numbers.
Find where most food waste happens.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–16 Food waste numbers; 16–20 Quick Challenge; 20–32 Language Focus 1–2; 32–38 Use: less food waste; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why must we collect old oil separately?
What is biodiesel?
Why is the number 61 percent surprising?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Biodiesel” and “At Home” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: fry, fuel, biodiesel, straw, lost, wasted.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the three numbers with the places missing.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short poster about old cooking oil.

formativeAssessment: Explains what happens to old oil.
Uses is called or is wasted correctly.
expectedResponses: Special centers change old oil into a clean fuel. This fuel is called biodiesel. Most food waste, 61 percent, happens at home.
content.transferTask: Write tips for less food waste at home.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners connect the numbers with their own homes?

rubricLevels.secure: Explains what happens to old oil.
Uses is called or is wasted.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners explain what happens to old cooking oil and where food is wasted. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A reads paragraph 1 and B reads paragraphs 2 and 3. Each tells the partner two facts.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads paragraph 3. Asker asks “Where does most food waste happen?” Checker checks the number.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A family member wants to pour old oil into the sink. The learner explains why not and what to do.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “This fuel is called biodiesel.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, what happens to old cooking oil and where most food is wasted. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “Most food waste happens at home. Why is this surprising?” (We can change it ourselves.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners explain biodiesel and give the three numbers 13, 17 and 61 percent.

thinkAloud.sentence: This fuel is called biodiesel.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: “Is called” gives a name. The sentence before tells me what the fuel is. Now I know the word for it. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “After we fry food, we have used oil.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: How much food waste happens at home?

onlineTask.post: Write two sentences: How can your family waste less food?
onlineTask.reply: Give your classmate one more idea.

objectives: Name electronic items that become waste.
Explain why batteries need special bins.
Name the metals in batteries.
Explain why recycling alone can’t solve the problem.
content.pedagogy: The chapter gives clear safety rules and then turns to the big idea of the book: recycling is not enough, so we need Zero Waste. A rule card (Never … / We must …) helps learners make a safety poster.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Batteries have chemicals that can get into soil and water.
Recycling is useful, but the chapter says it alone can’t solve the problem.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: imperatives · never + base verb · must · so (result)
Look (Activity 1): Never throw batteries in the normal trash!
Practise (Activity 2): choose never, must and special.
Likely errors: *Never to throw · *must putting.
Use (Activity 3): a safety poster.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: e-lec-TRON-ic, DAN-ger-ous, CHEM-i-cals, LITH-i-um, CO-balt, NICK-el.
beforeReading: Ask: “What do you do with old batteries?”
duringReading: First reading: Why do electronic waste and batteries need special bins?
Second reading: make a rule card.
Find why recycling alone can’t solve the problem.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–16 Rule card; 16–20 Quick Challenge; 20–32 Language Focus 1–2; 32–38 Use: a safety poster; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What do workers do with old machines?
Why must we never throw batteries in the trash?
What is the better idea at the end?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Electronic Waste” and “Battery Bins” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: electronic, dangerous, take apart, battery, chemicals, soil, solve.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the frame: Never … / We must …
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short paragraph about why we need Zero Waste.

formativeAssessment: Explains why batteries need special bins.
Explains why recycling is not enough.
expectedResponses: Never throw batteries in the normal trash. They have dangerous chemicals in them. Recycling needs a lot of energy and hard work, so recycling alone can’t solve the problem.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners see the turn from recycling to Zero Waste?

rubricLevels.secure: Explains why batteries need special bins.
Explains why recycling is not enough.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners explain why electronics and batteries need special bins. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: One learner reads paragraph 1 and the other reads paragraph 2. Each tells the partner why the waste is dangerous.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads paragraph 3. Asker asks “Why can recycling alone not solve the problem?” Checker finds the answer.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A friend wants to throw an old phone in the normal trash. The learner explains what to do.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “Never throw batteries in the normal trash!” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, why old phones and batteries need special bins. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “The chapter ends with ‘We need a better idea.’ Why?” (Recycling needs a lot of energy and work.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners give two reasons with “because” or “so” and name three metals.

thinkAloud.sentence: Electronic waste has dangerous materials in it, so we must put it in special bins.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: “So” shows a result. The danger is the reason. The special bins are the result. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “When they are old or broken, they become electronic waste.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: Which metals do special centers take out of batteries?

onlineTask.post: Write two sentences: Where can people put old batteries in your town?

objectives: Explain what Zero Waste means.
Explain why “zero” does not mean “no waste at all”.
Explain why waste is bad for health and nature.
Use try not to and again and again.
content.pedagogy: The chapter answers a common question: does zero waste mean no waste? A “Yes / No” starter clears up the idea. Learners then connect Zero Waste with their own habits.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Zero Waste does not mean no waste at all; it means making less trash.
“Try not to” puts “not” before “to”.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: try (not) to + base verb · again and again · means + -ing
Look (Activity 1): We try not to make waste.
Practise (Activity 2): fill make, again and valuable.
Likely errors: *try to not making · *don’t try make.
Use (Activity 3): I try not to.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Stress: CARE-ful-ly, VAL-u-a-ble, PROD-uct.
Sound: zero /ˈzɪroʊ/.
beforeReading: Ask: “Is it possible to make no waste at all?”
duringReading: First reading: What does Zero Waste mean?
Second reading: list what we do with Zero Waste.
Find why waste is bad.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–16 What we do; 16–20 Quick Challenge; 20–32 Language Focus 1–2; 32–38 Use: I try not to; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why is “no waste at all” not possible?
What is the whole life of a product?
How is waste bad for our health?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “A Way of Living” and “The Whole Life of a Product” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: zero, carefully, valuable, health.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the frame: Zero Waste means … We try …
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short definition of Zero Waste for younger learners.

expectedResponses: Zero Waste is a way of living. It means using things carefully and making less trash. Waste makes the air, water and soil dirty.
content.transferTask: Write about your Zero Waste habits.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners understand that Zero Waste is a way of living?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “try not to”.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners explain what Zero Waste means. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A reads paragraphs 1 and 2, B reads paragraph 3. Each tells the partner the main idea.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads paragraph 2. Asker asks “What do we try to do with Zero Waste?” Checker checks three actions.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A friend says, “Zero waste is impossible!” The learner explains what it really means.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “Zero Waste is a way of living.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, what Zero Waste really means. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “Why does the chapter start with a question?” (To correct a common wrong idea.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners explain that Zero Waste does not mean no waste and give two actions.

thinkAloud.strategy: Answer a question in the text
thinkAloud.sentence: Does “zero waste” mean “no waste at all”? No, that isn’t possible.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: The writer asks a question and answers it. The answer corrects a wrong idea. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “We all use things and make waste every day.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: What does Zero Waste mean?

onlineTask.post: Write two sentences about one Zero Waste habit you have.

objectives: Explain the linear economy.
Explain the circular economy.
Explain the main goal.
Use first, then and finally.
content.pedagogy: The chapter compares two models. Two diagrams on the board (a line and a circle) make the idea visual. Learners draw the life of one product in both models.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “Linear” means like a straight line; “circular” means like a circle.
The circular economy still lets the economy grow.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: first / then / finally · works like · doesn’t have to
Look (Activity 1): First, … Then … Finally, …
Practise (Activity 2): put the steps in order.
Likely errors: *Finally we throw them away first.
Use (Activity 3): a circle for a bottle.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: CIR-cu-lar, LIN-e-ar, e-CON-o-my.
beforeReading: Ask: “What is the difference between a line and a circle?”
duringReading: First reading: What is the old way?
Second reading: draw the line and the circle.
Find the main goal.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–16 Line and circle; 16–20 Quick Challenge; 20–32 Language Focus 1–2; 32–38 Use: a circle for a bottle; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What are the three steps of the old way?
How does nature work?
What is the main goal of a circular economy?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Take, Make, Throw Away” and “Like a Circle” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: economy, circular, linear, step, goal, grow.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the two diagrams with the first steps written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short paragraph that compares the two models.

expectedResponses: The old way has three steps. First, we take materials from nature. Then we make things. Finally, we throw them away. A circular economy works like a circle.
content.transferTask: Write about the life of a glass bottle.

exitTicket: Write the three steps of the old way.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners explain the difference between a linear and a circular economy. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A reads paragraph 2 and B reads paragraph 3. Each explains one kind of economy. Together they draw a line and a circle.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads paragraph 2. Asker asks “What are the three steps of the old way?” Checker checks them.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A younger child asks, “What is a circular economy?” The learner explains with the example of nature.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “The old way is like a line.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?

metadata.title: Zero Waste A2 — Teacher’s Book
metadata.subtitle: Our World Today
metadata.estimatedDuration: 11 chapter units of 40 minutes each. Whole-book review pages follow separately.
metadata.targetLearners: Young learners and adults who can read short, simple informational texts and write short connected sentences.
metadata.purpose: Develop A2 reading, listening, speaking and writing through a short informational text about waste and Zero Waste: kinds of waste and how they are recycled, why recycling alone is not enough, the circular economy, the three Rs, waste and climate, and what people and cities can do, using the Language Focus attached to every chapter.
metadata.approachDesc: Every chapter follows the TYMM route. YDAB1 listening and YDAB2 reading establish meaning; the Quick Challenge checks comprehension. Grammar is then learned in small steps: in the Language Focus, learners first LOOK at a form in a real chapter sentence, then PRACTISE it in controlled, meaningful tasks, and finally USE it in short YDAB3 speaking and YDAB4 writing about their own world.
metadata.assessmentEvidence: 11 Quick Challenges, text-evidence checks, chapter Language Focus tasks (Look → Practise → Use), exit tickets, Knowledge Check, Vocabulary Challenge, Language Review and Final Challenge.

formative: Short spoken and written Use tasks

readingFramework.before: Activate only what the chapter needs: a short question, a real object (a bottle, a carton, a battery) or a picture of a bin.
readingFramework.during: Listen first for gist (when the audio is ready), then read and follow the chapter’s own structure: a number card, a chart of materials, a pie chart, recycling steps, a rule card, a line and a circle or a list of ideas.
readingFramework.after: Complete the Quick Challenge, then the chapter’s Language Focus (look → practise → use), then a short production about the learners’ own world.

vocabularyApproach.selection: Word Notes are the bold words of the teacher-approved text. Prioritize them and the words needed for the chapter’s key idea.
vocabularyApproach.method: Infer meaning from context, a real object or a picture before any direct explanation.
vocabularyApproach.recycling: Reuse vocabulary in Language Focus tasks, exit tickets, Key Terms and the Language Review.

metadata.grammarApproach: Text-based and in small steps. Start from the chapter sentence, ask a simple meaning question (What does this word show?), let learners answer, then confirm the rule and practice it in context. Rule explanations appear in the app only after learners answer.
grammarSequence: Ch1: may + base verb · more than
Ch2: is made from · comes from · present simple for steps (sort → melt → make)
Ch3: past simple (recycled, burned, went, stayed) · percent · twice as much
Ch4: must + base verb · much less … than · be made of
Ch5: is called · is lost / is wasted · must
Ch6: imperatives · never + base verb · must · so (result)
Ch7: try (not) to + base verb · again and again · means + -ing
Ch8: first / then / finally · works like · doesn’t have to
Ch9: imperatives (Use less. Fix it.) · should · first / second / third
Ch10: when + present, present (cause and result) · twice as much as · fewer
Ch11: can + base verb (ideas) · so (result) · the best … is …

skillsFocus.listening: TYMM YDAB1: follow narration for gist, facts and numbers.
skillsFocus.reading: TYMM YDAB2: find key information, numbers, steps and simple reasons.
skillsFocus.speaking: TYMM YDAB3: describe habits, rules and simple plans in short connected sentences.
skillsFocus.writing: TYMM YDAB4: write short connected sentences with and, but, so and because.

valuesFocus: D16 Responsibility — Caring for nature and our shared world.
D5 Sensitivity — Noticing what nature needs.
D20 Helpfulness — Sharing and helping others.
D1 Justice — Thinking about people who suffer most.
languageFocus: Every one of the 11 chapters has a Language Focus set built as Look → Practise → Use (3 activities).
Use the Language Focus after basic comprehension and the Quick Challenge.
Always start from the story sentence and ask a meaning question before naming the form.
The Use step is connected spoken or written production about a new, non-story situation.
metadata.differentiationNotes: Reduce linguistic load without lowering the thinking target: one paragraph at a time, charts given in part, real objects, audio replay, sentence frames and oral rehearsal. Extend by asking for one more sentence or one more reason from the book, not by introducing outside facts.

sensitiveNotes.title: Source fidelity and respectful teaching
notes: Keep explanations within the wording of the book; do not add outside numbers or opinions.
Talk about food waste and money with care; some families may have little food at home.
Do not let learners touch real batteries or broken electronics in class; use pictures or closed, clean objects.

test.title: End-of-Level Test A2
test.when: Give the test when the class has finished the A2 books it reads this term. It has four parts and takes about 60 minutes plus a short speaking test for each learner.

metadata.title: Zero Waste A2 — Self-Study Guide
metadata.subtitle: Read • Find • Check • Build • Use
metadata.estimatedStudyTime: About 20 minutes per chapter, plus the review pages at the end
metadata.whoIsThisFor: A2 learners who read the text about Zero Waste alone or with a teacher.
learningGoals: Understand the 11 chapters of Zero Waste.
Find evidence in the text before answering.
Say how different kinds of waste are recycled.
Explain Zero Waste, the circular economy and the three Rs.
Use each chapter’s Language Focus in connected sentences.
recommendedUse: Study one chapter at a time.
Read (and listen, when the audio is ready) before the Quick Challenge.
Repair wrong answers with the text.
Do the Language Focus after you understand the chapter.
Do the review pages after Chapter 11.

readingDiary.intro: Keep this diary when you finish the book. Write short answers.
prompts: The date I finished the book:
My favorite chapter, and one reason:
One fact about waste that surprised me:
One sentence for a friend: “Read this book because …”
One new word I want to keep:
The next book I want to read in the library:

sections.title: 1. Make Your Plan
sections.text: This book has 11 chapters. Plan the whole book before Chapter 1.
points: Choose your study days and how many chapters you will read each week.
Write one personal goal for this book.
Save new words to My words and review them after one day, three days and one week.

sections.title: 2. One Chapter per Session
sections.text: Each chapter takes about 20 minutes. Open “Study Path” for the steps of your chapter.
points: Preview the title and the “Before You Read” question.
Read for the main idea.
Find the evidence.
Do the Quick Challenge.
Do the Language Focus.

sections.title: 3. Read and Listen
sections.text: Read every chapter twice: once for the main idea, once for the details. When the audio is ready, listen once while you follow the text.
points: First reading: What is the chapter about?
Second reading: Mark names, dates and linking words.
Say one long sentence aloud with the right pauses.

sections.title: 4. Word Notes
sections.text: Bold words have Word Notes. Use them after you have tried to understand the sentence yourself.
points: Guess the meaning from the sentence.
Check the Word Note.
Write the word in a new sentence of your own.

sections.title: 5. Quick Challenge
sections.text: Answer before you read the feedback. If you are wrong, repair the answer with the text.
points: Find the paragraph the question is about.
Read the key sentence again.
Explain why the right answer is right, then try again.

sections.title: 6. Language Focus
sections.text: Each chapter has 3 Language Focus activities built from the chapter’s own sentences.
points: Activity 1 (Notice): Look at a sentence and what it means.
Activities 2–3 (Build): Choose, complete, correct or rewrite forms.
Activity 4 (Use): Write or say connected sentences about a different situation.

sections.title: 7. When It Is Hard
sections.text: Some chapters have many names and dates. Change how you study, not your goal.
points: Read one paragraph only.
Make a time line of the dates.
List the names and what each one did.
Learn only three words today.

sections.title: 8. Values in the Book
sections.text: The book shows responsibility, sensitivity, helpfulness and justice. Find the sentence first, then think of a small action of your own.
points: Responsibility: Responsibility: Never throw batteries in the normal trash; we must put them in battery bins (Chapter 6).
Sensitivity: Sensitivity: In nature, nothing is wasted (Chapter 8).
Helpfulness: Helpfulness: Tool libraries let people borrow tools instead of buying them (Chapter 11).
Justice: Justice: Many poorer countries make very little greenhouse gas but suffer the most from climate change (Chapter 10).

sections.title: 9. At the End of the Book
sections.text: After Chapter 11, do the review pages in this order. Go back to a chapter when an answer is not clear.
points: Key Facts
Knowledge Check
Vocabulary Challenge
Master Glossary
Key Terms
Language Review
Final Challenge

sections.title: 10. Look Back
sections.text: Before Chapter 1 and again at the end, answer the “I can” statements of a few chapters. What can you do now that you could not do before?
points: Which chapter changed what you knew?
Tell someone at home in four sentences what Zero Waste means, in your home language or in English.
